oneSentence: A reference method or result used to judge how a model performs against a relevant starting point.
plainExplanation:
A baseline is a reference method or score that gives you something to compare against. It tells you, “With this reference approach, this is the result.” Then you compare the new system against that result.

What goes in is a task, some data and a rule for scoring performance. The rule for scoring is an evaluation metric, such as accuracy or recall. You also choose a relevant reference method, for example predicting the most common class, using keyword search, repeating the previous value or using the current process.

What happens is that you run this reference method on the same task that the new model will face. What comes out is a reference score, such as 80% accuracy, plus a clearer sense of how hard the task may be.

This matters because a score can look impressive without meaning much. If 80% of documents are routine, a system that always says “routine” gets 80% accuracy without finding anything unusual. A new model scoring 82% may sound better, but it may add little practical value.

Baseline does not mean benchmark. A benchmark is a standard test set-up used to compare systems on a defined task under stated conditions. A baseline is a reference method or result used within an evaluation. A benchmark can report several baselines.

everydayAnalogy.title: Checking whether search helps at all
everydayAnalogy.story: A team in Nairobi needs to find policy documents about flood preparedness in a large shared folder. First, one colleague tries the simplest method: search for the exact phrase “flood preparedness” and open the first ten results. They record that 4 of the 10 documents are actually useful. Then another colleague uses a better search tool that expands related terms such as “early warning” and “risk reduction” and finds 7 useful documents out of 10. The first result gives the team a starting point, so they can tell whether the new tool really improves the search.

everydayAnalogy.limitation: Real model baselines can be more varied than one simple manual search. Some baselines are statistical rules, historical averages or previously deployed systems, not just a weaker version of the same tool. Also, a real evaluation may use several metrics at once, while the story uses one easy count of useful documents.

visual.title: Baseline versus new model
visual.learningObjective: Show that a model score only becomes meaningful when compared with a simple, relevant reference result.
visual.description: Two side-by-side paths compare a simple baseline with a new model on the same task and data, then bring both scores together for interpretation. Read left to right: same input, different methods, then a decision about whether the improvement is large and useful enough to matter.

steps.label: Same task
steps.explanation: Start with one clearly defined task, one evaluation dataset and one scoring rule so the comparison is fair.
steps.visualInstruction: At the left, draw one shared input box labelled 'Same task + same test data + same metric'. Split one arrow into two equal branches.

steps.label: Simple reference
steps.explanation: On the top branch, run a very simple method such as predicting the most common class or using exact keywords.
steps.visualInstruction: Top branch box labelled 'Baseline method'. Add small note text: 'simple, cheap, reasonable'.

steps.label: New system
steps.explanation: On the bottom branch, run the model or tool you want to assess.
steps.visualInstruction: Bottom branch box labelled 'New model or system'. Add small note text: 'more complex approach'.

steps.label: Compare scores
steps.explanation: Bring the two outputs together and compare their scores, not just the new score by itself.
steps.visualInstruction: Merge both branches into one comparison box showing example numbers such as 'Baseline: 80%' and 'New: 82%'.

steps.label: Interpret carefully
steps.explanation: Ask whether the improvement is meaningful for the real use case, given errors, costs and risks.
steps.visualInstruction: Final box on the right labelled 'Useful improvement?'. Under it, show three short checks: 'better enough?', 'safer?', 'worth the cost?'.

visual.interaction: Hovering over the comparison box reveals alternative baseline examples such as 'majority class', 'random guess', 'keyword search' and 'previous system'.
visual.accessibilityDescription: The diagram compares two approaches using the same task, data and metric. A shared starting box splits into two branches. The top branch is a simple baseline method, described as simple, cheap and reasonable. The bottom branch is the new model or system. Both branches produce scores that meet in one comparison box, with example values Baseline 80% and New 82%. A final box asks whether the improvement is useful, with checks for whether it is large enough, safer and worth the cost. The main lesson is that a model score means little without a relevant reference point.
visual.reducedMotionDescription: A static side-by-side comparison shows one shared input feeding a baseline branch and a new model branch, then a box comparing their scores and a final box asking whether the difference is useful in practice.

workedExample.scenario: A desk officer in a regional bureau is finalising the evaluation annex for a document-routing pilot. The classifier assigns 300 public programme summaries to education, health or climate queues.
workedExample.input: Test set of 300 summaries: 180 health, 90 education and 30 climate.
process: Set the baseline to always predict the most frequent class, health.
Score that baseline on the fixed test set using the evaluation metric selected for the pilot.
Run the candidate classifier on the same test set and score it with the same metric.
Compare overall accuracy and class-level recall, particularly for the less frequent education and climate categories.
workedExample.result: The majority-class baseline is correct for 180 of 300 summaries, giving 60% accuracy. The classifier reaches 72%, an improvement of 12 percentage points. That gain is not sufficient on its own: if climate recall remains poor, the classifier may still be unsuitable for routing work.

unWorkplaceExample.scenario: A legal officer in an inter-agency secretariat is drafting a lessons-learned note after a pilot that grouped comments on draft guidance by legal issue. Before the findings go to the front office, the officer compares the model with the keyword rules previously used for first-pass sorting.
unWorkplaceExample.relevance: The keyword rules are a useful baseline only if they and the model are assessed on the same labelled comments, with the same categories and metric. The comparison shows whether the pilot improved on the existing workflow rather than merely producing a respectable-looking score.
unWorkplaceExample.caution: Comments on draft guidance may contain confidential or legally sensitive material. They must not be entered into a tool that has not been approved for that material. Use an approved environment, minimise the text retained and keep legal review in the workflow.

whyItMatters: Without a baseline, people can be impressed by numbers that do not prove real usefulness. A high score may simply reflect an easy dataset, an imbalanced class distribution or a weak comparison. Baselines help non-specialists ask better questions: Is this system better than a simple rule? Better than the current process? Better in the ways that matter for risk, cost and fairness? This supports safer procurement, clearer reporting and more reliable decisions about whether to deploy, revise or reject a system.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: A baseline must be very weak, such as random guessing.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Not always. A useful baseline should be simple but relevant. For some tasks, random guessing is too weak to teach much. A stronger baseline, such as the current manual process or a straightforward keyword rule, can give a more honest test of whether the new system is worth adopting.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: If a model beats the baseline, it is ready for use.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Beating a baseline only shows improvement over that reference point. The model may still be inaccurate, unreliable on rare cases, badly calibrated or unsafe for the setting. You still need to check error types, robustness, human oversight needs and whether the performance is good enough for the real consequences of mistakes.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Baseline and benchmark mean the same thing.
commonMisconceptions.correction: They are related but not identical. A baseline is the reference result from a simple method or existing process. A benchmark is often the standard dataset or test suite used for comparison. A single benchmark can include several baselines.

simpleVsTechnical.simple: A baseline is the reference result you compare against before calling a model better.
simpleVsTechnical.technical: In model evaluation, a baseline is a reference method or performance level assessed under the same task definition, data split and evaluation metric as the candidate model. Common baselines include majority-class prediction, random prediction with known class frequencies, linear or rule-based methods, historical averages, previous production systems and human performance under defined conditions. The purpose is to compare the model with trivial patterns or an existing workflow. A baseline can reveal that an apparently high score offers little improvement over an obvious strategy, but it does not by itself diagnose problems such as data leakage. Baseline selection depends on context. For time series, a last-value or seasonal baseline may be appropriate. For retrieval, keyword search may be relevant. For classification, majority-class or simple linear models are common. A strong evaluation may report multiple baselines because one rarely captures every practical comparison.

keyTakeaway: A baseline makes a model score meaningful, provided both are tested on the same task, data split and metric.

quickCheck.question: Why is a baseline useful when evaluating a classifier?
options: It guarantees the model will generalise to future data.
It shows whether the model improves on a simple, reasonable reference method.
It replaces the need to inspect false positives and false negatives.
It makes accuracy the only metric you need.
quickCheck.explanation: A baseline shows whether a model improves on a relevant reference method. It is not a required performance threshold, a standard test set-up or the accuracy metric itself.

issues.problem: The page repeatedly defines a baseline as necessarily simple or easy. That contradicts its own examples of previous production systems and human performance, which may be strong or complex references. The one-sentence definition also says comparison with a baseline establishes “real value”, but a score comparison alone does not establish practical value.
issues.fix: Define a baseline as a relevant reference method or performance level. Describe simple rules as common examples, not as a defining requirement. Do not claim that beating one proves practical value.

issues.problem: The benchmark distinction is inaccurate because it reduces a benchmark to a dataset or test suite. The supplied definition is a standard test set-up with a defined task and stated conditions. A dataset alone is not necessarily a benchmark.
issues.fix: Replace the distinction with: “A benchmark is a standard test set-up used to compare systems on a defined task under stated conditions. A baseline is a reference method or result used within an evaluation. A benchmark can report several baselines.”

issues.problem: The technical explanation again requires a “simple” method while listing previous production systems and human performance. It also claims a baseline helps determine whether a score reflects data leakage. Comparing with a baseline does not by itself detect or diagnose leakage.
issues.fix: Define the baseline as a reference method or performance level, and say that it contextualises performance. Remove data leakage from the list of things a baseline can diagnose.

issues.problem: The arithmetic is correct: 180/300 = 0.60 = 60%, and 72% - 60% = 12 percentage points. However, “so the model adds value” does not follow from that arithmetic. It establishes higher overall accuracy, not practical value, acceptable minority-class performance or readiness for use.
issues.fix: Baseline accuracy is 180/300 = 60%. The new classifier reaches 72% accuracy, which is 12 percentage points higher. This shows improvement in overall accuracy, but does not by itself prove practical value. If its climate recall is still very low, the team may decide it is not yet good enough for the real task.

issues.problem: Option 0 is false because a baseline cannot guarantee generalisation. Option 1 is correct. Option 2 is false because a baseline does not replace error inspection. Option 3 is false because it does not make accuracy the only metric. Although only option 1 is defensible, the other three use obvious absolute claims such as “guarantees”, “replaces” and “only”, so the answer can be selected without understanding baselines.
issues.fix: Keep the question and correct index, but replace the options with: [“It defines the performance threshold the classifier must meet.”, “It shows whether the model improves on a relevant reference method.”, “It supplies the standard test set-up used to compare systems.”, “It gives the share of test cases labelled correctly.”]. These distinguish baseline from a threshold, benchmark and accuracy.
